note: The product structure. Three real levels, not one flat variant row. The level an attribute belongs to is the whole point: colour does not belong on a size, price does not belong on a design, and a size that carries its own colour name will contradict itself the first time somebody edits one of them.

hierarchy.plain: The design itself, before you choose a colour or a size.
hierarchy.keyed_by: style_id — the retailer's own design number
hierarchy.beauty: A foundation line, e.g. 'Soft Matte Blurring Foundation'
hierarchy.food: 'Crispy Chicken Burger' as a menu item
hierarchy.why: Competitors move prices at this level, not SKU by SKU. Reporting a price change 14 times because a shirt comes in 14 sizes is how an alerting system gets muted in week one.

hierarchy.plain: The design in one particular colour or shade. This is what gets photographed and what a product page usually shows.
hierarchy.food: Usually not applicable; a recipe variant where it is
hierarchy.why: It is the level shoppers actually browse, the level images and ratings attach to, and the level at which a shade or colourway can be discontinued on its own. Beauty lives almost entirely here — a foundation in the wrong shade is a different product, not a variation.

hierarchy.plain: The exact thing with a barcode and a stock figure. A colour in a size.
hierarchy.keyed_by: style_id + colour_code + size_code, and a GTIN where one exists
hierarchy.fashion: The light blue shirt in medium
hierarchy.food: The burger as a regular, or as a combo
hierarchy.why: The only level where stock is real. Availability, size-run gaps and barcode matching all live here and nowhere else.

hierarchy.plain: That variant, at one shop, in one country, on one delivery app, at one moment.
hierarchy.keyed_by: variant + retailer + market + seller + channel + observed_at
hierarchy.fashion: The medium shirt on Namshi today
hierarchy.why: Price is never a property of a product. It is a property of a product in a place at a time, which is why it sits here and not on the variant.

grouping_rules.rule: Group by style ID WITHIN a retailer, never across retailers.
grouping_rules.why: A style number is the retailer's internal design code. H&M's 0979945 means nothing to Zara. Treating two retailers' style numbers as comparable would merge unrelated products silently.

grouping_rules.rule: Across retailers, branded goods group by GTIN; own-label groups by nothing at all.
grouping_rules.why: This is the structural reason own-label fashion needs an agreed basket. There is no shared key, and no amount of attribute matching invents one.

grouping_rules.rule: A retailer's style ID is the single strongest free grouping key we get.
grouping_rules.why: It is published on the page, it is stable, and it collapses a 60-row size grid into one product. Capture it on every reading even when we cannot yet use it.

grouping_rules.rule: Where a retailer exposes no style ID, derive one and mark it derived.
grouping_rules.why: A derived grouping is useful and must never be mistaken for the retailer's own. Derived groupings are rebuilt when the rule changes; captured ones are not.

grouping_rules.rule: Match once at style or colour level, then inherit to every size beneath it.
grouping_rules.why: Matching 14 sizes separately costs 14 times as much and produces 14 chances to disagree with itself. One shirt cannot be both matched and unmatched.

grouping_rules.rule: Roll a price up from variants to a style only with the rule named on screen.
grouping_rules.why: A style has no single price. It has a cheapest size, a median size and a most-common size, and those are three different numbers that a reader will assume is one.

grouping_rules.rule: Never collapse the levels into one wide table 'for convenience'.
grouping_rules.why: The first edit that sets a colour name on a size row creates a product that contradicts itself, and nothing in the system can tell which of the two rows is right.

attribute_groups.plain: Technical facts about the page we read, which make the reading reproducible.

attribute_storage.decision: Common attributes are real columns. Vertical-specific ones live in a defined attribute table with a registry, not in a free-form blob.
attribute_storage.why: A jsonb blob accepts 'colour', 'color', 'Colour' and 'col' on four consecutive days and nothing complains. Every attribute-based comparison then quietly reads a fraction of the data and reports a confident number from it.
rules: Every attribute must exist in the registry before a value can be written against it. An unregistered key is rejected, not stored.
The registry fixes the level an attribute belongs to. A value written at the wrong level is rejected — colour cannot be set on a size.
Enumerated attributes have their allowed values listed. A new value raises a review item rather than being accepted silently.
Raw retailer text is kept alongside the normalised value, always. Normalisation is a reading, and we must be able to show the original when somebody disputes it.
Completeness is measured per attribute per retailer and shown next to anything derived from it.

capture_principle.rule: Capture everything the page offers on the first pass, store it raw, and parse later.
capture_principle.why: A second visit is a second chance to be blocked, and tomorrow's page will not show today's price, badge or promotion. Collection is the expensive, fragile, unrepeatable step; parsing is cheap and can be redone a hundred times over stored captures. Anything not taken on the first pass is gone for good.
consequences: Prefer the machine-readable block the retailer already publishes over reading rendered text. It is what the shop itself asserts and it breaks far less often.
Store the whole specification block unparsed even where no extractor exists yet.
Record what we expected to find and did not, per reading, so a half-parsed page is a defect rather than a quiet success.
Detect page template changes automatically. A redesign breaks every parser at once, and without detection it is a silent week of wrong data.

detail_only_meaning.rule: An attribute marked detail-only is shown on the product page and carried in the export, but no analytic screen aggregates it.
detail_only_meaning.why: Most descriptive fields earn their place twice over without ever becoming a chart: they are how a buyer recognises the product, they are what makes a basket line enforceable, and they are what the matching engine compares when there is no barcode. Marking them keeps that deliberate. The alternative is a registry where nobody can tell a field with a purpose from one somebody added and forgot.
detail_only_meaning.consequence: A newly added attribute is neither on an analytic screen nor marked, so it fails the build until somebody decides which it is. That is the point: the decision gets made once, when the field is added, rather than never.
